newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Sumitomo copper king met his match in funds.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Sumitomo copper king met his match in funds.

text.p: Scrap dealer Herbert Black of Canada, whose selling of copper helped topple one-time Japanese metals idol Yasuo Hamanaka, said on Monday he thought the former Sumitomo Corp trader may have underestimated the weight of big speculative funds. Hamanaka was sacked by Sumitomo in June for running up losses then estimated at $1.8 billion from unauthorised trading in copper. The losses have since swelled to $2.6 billion.
Hamanaka's exerted a grip on the market far greater than anyone realised, and inflated the price of copper, Black said.
"The last three years were a total lie, the market should never have been where it was," he told a metals industry lunch in London.
But in the summer last year the big funds took Hamanaka on by selling vast amounts of copper they did not own, forcing the Japanese trader to keep buying copper to prop up prices.
"Hamanaka did not realise how big the major funds were," Black said.

Key players in the world's industrial metals industry are meeting in London this week for their annual London Metal Exchange week of events. Black said he thought from the middle of last year that copper prices were too high and joined the funds in selling the market short. The Canadian trader initially got his fingers burned.
But a return fight by Black and the funds in June this year finally toppled Hamanaka, earning Black millions of dollars.
Black insisted he had no prior knowledge of Sumitomo's woes.
Copper prices went into freefall and have levelled out, but Black said Sumitomo still holds 500,000 tonnes of copper. He forecast prices would head lower and that Sumitomo's losses would mount.
"I would say total loss is $3 billion to $4 billion," Black said.
His comments added to the gloom already shrouding the world's industrial metals markets, sending copper briefly lower in afternoon trading on the LME Monday, later recovering to about $1,900 a tonne.
Added to Sumitomo's hoard, Black said there was a further 180,000 tonnes of copper stashed away in warehouses in China.
Sumitomo's copper holdings, coupled with China's hoard and new production coming on stream will push prices down to $1,600 a tonne next year and $1,400 in 1998, Black said.
Many fingers were pointed in anger at the LME when the Sumitomo scandal broke, but Black said whatever the rules, a rogue trader would try to break them.
British regulatory watchdog, the Securities and Investments Board, is probing the LME to see if changes in its trading rules are needed.
Black suggested there was a conflict of interest at the heart of the LME whose board members work for companies who deal in metals.
"There is such a conflict there. We have to have fair representation," Black said.
The scandal could have been avoided if the LME had stepped in to stop the premium the cash market commanded over forward months prices -- normally a sign of a tight market -- until metal stocks fell.

David King, LME chief executive, said he was unable to give a full account of events while investigations continued. "We know a lot of what was behind the scenes...We can't control certain elements of the market," King said.

Black said the biggest winners were the copper producers who bought options, from Sumitomo and a clutch of banks, to protect the price of metal they mined. After prices tumbled, producers sold back those options to cream off millions of dollars for their company coffers.

Codelco, the state-owned Chilean copper producer, who also lost millions of dollars in trading, did business with Sumitomo, Black said. This helped to keep spot prices firm but Black saw no clear link between the two companies.
